replies.author: @HiddenCanada
replies.text: The added grain is just a stylistic treatment to help the archival visuals feel consistent with the period, it isn’t meant to make anything look more “genuine” than it is. The historical claims in the video are based on documented sources, not the visual texture.

comments.author: @sylviagrznar8414
comments.text: The SS Keewatin is an intact Edwardian/Titanic era steam ship you can visit in Kingston ON so your intro needs to be corrected

replies.author: @dac762-n9v
replies.text:
@Hid@HiddenCanada
Parks Canada, sadly, isn’t always a great source. They’re getting better, but sometimes it seems like they just got computers last month. I would always double check their interpretations before repeating them.

replies.author: @HiddenCanada
replies.text: Good catch. The wording in the video actually comes from Parks Canada’s National Historic Site designation, which describes the Empress wreck as the “sole surviving marine component” of Canadian Pacific’s prewar transportation network. But you’re absolutely right that the SS Keewatin survives intact in Kingston and was a Canadian Pacific Great Lakes passenger steamship built in 1907. So that Parks Canada wording can definitely sound misleading without the extra context. I have put the correction in description as well. Appreciate you pointing it out.

comments.author: @patrick-c8d7r
comments.text: Biggest maritime disaster, more dead than the Titanic , no movies made about her .

replies.author: @HiddenCanada
replies.text: That’s the part that surprised me too. Small correction though: the Empress had more passenger deaths than Titanic, 840 vs. 832, but Titanic’s total death toll was higher once crew are included. Still amazing how little attention the Empress gets compared with Titanic, especially considering how fast she went down. And yeah, no huge Hollywood film has really put her story into popular culture the same way.
